segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Am I not free? Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord? Are you not my work in the Lord?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If to others I am not an apostle, to you at least I am; for you are the seal of my apostleship in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is my defense to those who are examining me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do we not have the right to eat and drink?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do we not have the right to take along a believing wife, as the other apostles do, and the Lord’s brothers, and Cephas?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Or is it only Barnabas and I who have no right to refrain from working?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who ever serves as a soldier at his own expense? Who plants a vineyard and does not eat its fruit? Who shepherds a flock and does not have some of the flock’s milk?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Am I saying this from a merely human standpoint, or does the law not say the same?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in the law of Moses it is written:

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Is it the oxen God cares about,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: or is he surely speaking for our sake? Yes, it was written for our sake, because the plowman ought to plow in hope, and the thresher to thresh in hope of having a share.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If we sowed spiritual things for you, is it a great matter if we reap material things from you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If others share this right over you, do we not even more? But we did not make use of this right. Instead we put up with everything, so as not to put any obstacle in the way of the good news of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you not know that those who work in the temple service eat what comes from the temple, and those who attend at the altar share in what is offered on the altar?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way the Lord also directed that those who proclaim the good news should live from the good news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But I have made use of none of these things. And I am not writing this so that it may be done that way in my case. For I would rather die than— no one will empty my boast!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I proclaim the good news, I have no boast in that, for necessity presses on me; woe to me if I do not proclaim the good news!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I do this by my own choice, I have a wage; but if not by my own choice, I have been entrusted with a stewardship.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then is my wage? That in proclaiming the good news I may offer the good news free of charge, so as not to make full use of my right in the good news.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For though I am free from all, I have made myself a slave to all, so that I might win more of them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To the Jews I became as a Jew, so that I might win Jews; to those under the law as one under the law, though I myself am not under the law, so that I might win those under the law;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: to those outside the law as one outside the law, though I am not outside God’s law but inside Christ’s law, so that I might win those outside the law.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To the weak I became weak, so that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all people, so that by all means I might save some.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I do everything for the sake of the good news, so that I may become a partner in it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you not know that the runners in a stadium all run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may seize it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone who competes exercises self-control in everything. They do it to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable one.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So that is how I run: not aimlessly. That is how I box: not as one beating the air.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: No, I batter my body and make it my slave, so that after preaching to others I myself may not be disqualified.

notes.note: The Greek is literally “a sister, a wife”, where “sister” means a fellow believer, as “brother” does throughout the letter. The second word can mean either “woman” or “wife”, and some early interpreters took the phrase to mean a Christian woman who travelled as an assistant. Nearly all modern scholars read it as a wife who is a believer, supported at the churches’ expense along with her husband.

notes.phrase: You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.
notes.note: The quotation is Deuteronomy 25:4. Grain was threshed by driving oxen over the cut stalks, and the law let the animal eat as it worked. Paul argues from the lesser case to the greater, a common form of reasoning among Jewish interpreters of the time.

The Greek adverb can mean “certainly” or “entirely”. On the second reading Paul would be saying the law was written wholly for people and not for oxen at all. On the reading adopted here he says only that it undoubtedly applies to human workers as well.

“Gospel” has become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations, and that is what Paul’s readers heard. Many modern translations already alternate between “gospel” and “good news”.

Paul appeals to an instruction of Jesus. It is usually identified with the saying preserved in the Gospels that the worker deserves his wages or food, given when Jesus sent out his disciples (Luke 10:7; Matthew 10:10). This is one of the few places where Paul cites Jesus’s teaching directly.

notes.phrase: than— no one will empty my boast!
notes.traditional: than have anyone deprive me of my ground for boasting
notes.note: In the earliest manuscripts Paul’s sentence breaks off and restarts, apparently under the pressure of feeling. Many later manuscripts smooth it into “than that anyone should make my boast empty”, and most English versions translate the smoothed sense. The broken sentence is kept here as the editors print it.

The Greek word is the ordinary term for a worker’s pay, and the whole chapter is about whether Paul may be paid for his work. “Reward” is the traditional rendering and is not wrong. “Wage” keeps the paradox of the next verse in view: Paul’s pay is to work without pay.

A steward managed a household or estate for its owner and was very often a slave, who did what he was assigned and was owed no wages for it. Paul’s point is that his preaching is a charge laid on him, not a job he chose. Some punctuate differently, running this clause into the next verse: “if not by my own choice I have been entrusted with a stewardship, what then is my wage?”

Paul plays on two adjectives, literally “law-less” and “in-law”, each followed by a bare genitive: “not lawless of God but in-law of Christ”. The traditional “under the law of Christ” borrows the phrase “under the law” that Paul has just said does not apply to him, and blurs the contrast. The genitives could also be read as “toward God” and “toward Christ”, and what “Christ’s law” covers is debated.

notes.traditional: share with them in its blessings
notes.note: The Greek says only “a joint partner of it”, meaning of the good news. Most translations supply “blessings”, taking Paul to mean that he hopes to share in the salvation the good news brings. Others take him to mean a partner in its work and progress, and the rendering leaves both open.

Corinth oversaw the Isthmian Games, held every two years nearby and among the major athletic festivals of the Greek world. The victor’s prize was a wreath of foliage, pine or celery, which soon withered. Competitors trained under strict discipline before the games, which is the self-control Paul refers to.

The verb literally means to strike someone under the eye, to give a black eye, and it continues the boxing image of the previous verse. Most modern translations soften it to “discipline” or “keep under control”. Paul is speaking figuratively of rigorous self-mastery, not of self-harm, but the image he uses is a boxer’s blow.

candidates.reason: Recurs across the New Testament as “authority”, “power” or “right”, and readers would be misled if the choice varied without a rule.
The ordinary word for pay, traditionally rendered “reward” in sayings of Jesus and in Paul; a single policy on “wage/pay” versus “reward” is needed.
“Preach” now suggests a sermon, whereas the Greek means to proclaim as a herald; the choice needs to be coordinated with εὐαγγελίζω and καταγγέλλω.
The boasting word group is frequent in Paul and is rendered variously as “boast”, “pride”, “glory” or “ground for boasting”; consistency matters for following his argument.
The sibling terms for fellow believers (ἀδελφός/ἀδελφή) occur throughout the letters and need one policy on “brother/sister”, “brothers and sisters” or “believer”.

warnings: Verse 17: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.
